title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — drowning grasp; Greek 'enter judgment' ≠ begin-to-be
pass_a_gloss: PLAC: Like drowning men the learned man seizes whatever floats—but in vain. Grant that among the Greeks εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν means to begin a suit: does the same verb with any other noun mean 'begin'? Will εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον or εἰς τὴν πόλιν mean to begin a house or city, or to begin being in house or city as if you were not there before?
pass_b_english: PLAC. After the manner of those who are drowning, the learned man seizes whatever meets him: but in vain. For grant that the phrase eis to dikasterion eiselthein among the Greeks signifies to begin a suit, does it follow that the same verb constructed with any other noun is used for 'to begin'? Will, for example, eiselthein eis ton oikon, or eis ten polin, be to begin a house or a city, or so to begin to be in a house or city, that you were not there before?
source_text: PLAC. More eorum qui submerguntur, obvium quodque arripit vir doctus: sed frustra. Significet enim phrasis εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν apud Graecos incipere litem, num sequitur, idem verbum cum quovis alio nomine constructum pro incipere usurpari? Num ex. g. εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον, vel εἰς τὴν πόλιν, erit incipere domum vel urbem, aut ita incipere esse in domo vel urbe, ut antea non fueris?

lemmas.gloss: after the manner of those who drown

choices.choice: Judgment-enter idiom does not generalize to begin-to-be
